BUSS1020 Week 09

BUSS1020 Week 9 — Independent Two-Sample Inference and Pooled Variance

Comparing populations

Two-sample inference compares population characteristics using samples from two groups. The main designs are independent-sample comparisons of means, related-sample comparisons of means, and comparisons of proportions. Comparing two population variances is a distinct problem from comparing means; a regression overall F test is also a different procedure.

Independent samples arise when observations in one sample are not paired with or statistically dependent on observations in the other. Related samples arise from repeated observations on the same units or deliberately matched units. Choosing a method begins with the sampling design, not merely the fact that there are two columns of numbers.

For population means μ₁ and μ₂, the parameter of interest is μ₁ − μ₂. Subscripts 1 and 2 identify the groups. The estimator is X̄₁ − X̄₂, where X̄ⱼ denotes the random sample mean for group j. Its expectation is μ₁ − μ₂, so it is unbiased.

For independent samples of sizes n₁ and n₂ with population variances σ₁² and σ₂²:

Var(X̄₁ − X̄₂) = σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂.

The standard error is the square root of this variance. Uncertainty adds even though the means are subtracted: independence makes the covariance term zero, not the individual variances negative.

Hypotheses and decision rules

Let Δ₀ be the hypothesised difference. For equal means, Δ₀ = 0. The null is H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = Δ₀; the alternative specifies a difference below, above or unequal to Δ₀.

Let t* denote a positive t critical magnitude for the specified degrees of freedom and significance level α. For a one-sided test it is the 1 − α percentile; for a two-sided test it is the 1 − α/2 percentile.

Alternative

Rejection rule

μ₁ − μ₂ < Δ₀

t < −t*

μ₁ − μ₂ > Δ₀

t > t*

μ₁ − μ₂ ≠ Δ₀

Writing μ₁ = μ₂ is equivalent to μ₁ − μ₂ = 0. The subtraction order must remain consistent in the hypotheses, estimate, statistic and interpretation.

Choosing between pooled and separate variance

When both population standard deviations are unknown, sample standard deviations s₁ and s₂ estimate them.

• If the population variances can reasonably be assumed equal, pool the sample variances to estimate one common variance.

• If equal variances are not assumed, keep the variance estimates separate and use Welch's method.

The pooled procedure requires random independent samples and equal population variances. Exact small-sample t inference assumes normal populations. With appropriate non-normal populations, large samples can support an approximation. Practical guidelines are both samples at least 30, or both at least 15 for reasonably symmetric populations. These thresholds are not universal protection against severe skewness or influential observations.

Pooled variance and test statistic

The sample variance sⱼ² measures variation within group j. Each contributes nⱼ − 1 degrees of freedom. Their degrees-of-freedom-weighted average is:

sₚ² = [(n₁ − 1)s₁² + (n₂ − 1)s₂²]/(n₁ + n₂ − 2).

The subscript p denotes pooling. The pooled standard deviation is sₚ = √sₚ². The estimated standard error of the mean difference is:

SE = √[sₚ²(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)].

The test statistic is:

t = [(x̄₁ − x̄₂) − Δ₀]/SE, with df = n₁ + n₂ − 2.

Lowercase x̄₁ and x̄₂ are the observed sample means. Under the equal-means null, Δ₀ = 0. The degrees of freedom add because the two within-group variance estimates contribute n₁ − 1 and n₂ − 1 independent degrees of freedom under the model.

For a two-sided test, the p-value is 2P(T ≥ |t|), where T has the specified null t distribution. Reject if it is below α; otherwise fail to reject.

Confidence interval for the difference

The matching two-sided 1 − α confidence interval is:

(x̄₁ − x̄₂) ± t√[sₚ²(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)].*

Here t* is the 1 − α/2 percentile with n₁ + n₂ − 2 degrees of freedom. The interval estimates a population mean difference, not an individual observation. In repeated sampling, the procedure covers the true fixed difference with probability 1 − α.

If the interval excludes zero, the matching two-sided equal-means test rejects. A wholly positive interval supports a positive population difference; a wholly negative interval supports a negative difference. A two-sided test is formulated as evidence of a difference, while its sign and interval supply the direction and size of the estimated association.

Worked example — NYSE and NASDAQ dividend yields

Compare mean dividend yields with the equal-variance assumption:

Group

Sample size

Sample mean yield

Sample standard deviation

NYSE, group 1

21

3.27%

1.30 percentage points

NASDAQ, group 2

25

2.53%

1.16 percentage points

Test H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 against H₁: μ₁ − μ₂ ≠ 0 at α = 0.05. Calculations use percentage-point units, so the estimate is 3.27 − 2.53 = 0.74 percentage points.

Compute the pooled variance: sₚ² = [20(1.30²) + 24(1.16²)]/44 = (33.80 + 32.2944)/44 = 1.502145, approximately 1.5021.

Compute the standard error: SE = √[1.502145(1/21 + 1/25)] ≈ 0.3628 percentage points.

Compute the statistic: t = 0.74/0.3628 ≈ 2.040.

Degrees of freedom are 21 + 25 − 2 = 44. The two-sided 5% critical values are ±2.0154.

Because 2.040 > 2.0154, reject H₀. The two-sided p-value is approximately 0.047, just below 0.05.

The matching 95% interval is:

0.74 ± 2.0154(0.3628) ≈ 0.009 to 1.471 percentage points.

It is narrowly above zero, indicating evidence of a larger mean NYSE yield under the pooled model. It is a close decision, so retain precision until after comparison with α.

Both samples are below 30, making approximate inference particularly dependent on a reasonable population-shape assumption such as symmetry. Using Welch's method on these same summaries instead gives t ≈ 2.0193, df ≈ 40.5744 and a two-sided p-value near 0.0501, resulting in non-rejection at 5%. This difference is a consequence of the model and standard-error calculation; the pooled conclusion must not be substituted for the unequal-variance conclusion.

Excel implementation

• T.TEST(array1,array2,tails,2) implements an equal-variance two-sample test; tails=2 requests a two-sided p-value.

• T.INV.2T(alpha,df) gives the positive two-sided critical magnitude; T.INV(1-alpha/2,df) is equivalent.

• T.DIST.2T(ABS(t),df) gives the two-sided p-value from a calculated statistic.

• In Data Analysis, choose t-Test: Two-Sample Assuming Equal Variances and specify the two ranges, null difference and α.

A one-sided directional question requires retaining the statistic's sign and selecting the appropriate tail; an absolute difference alone does not establish the desired direction.
